title: Google AI detects high blood pressure from a regular smartwatch
dek: A Google Research model uses pulse and motion sensors to spot signs of hypertension; it’s live in the Google Health app but not a diagnostic tool.
body:
Google Research built an algorithm that can detect signs of high blood pressure using only the pulse and motion sensors in a standard smartwatch , no blood-pressure cuff required. In a 196-person study the system achieved a 65.8% detection rate, which the team reported as better than the traditional in‑office measurement. The feature is already available in the Google Health app, with Google saying it does not replace a formal diagnosis.

## Why it matters

High blood pressure is a common clinical condition that typically requires cuff-based measurements for diagnosis. A cuffless method that runs on widely used smartwatches could expand screening reach because it uses sensors many wearables already include: pulse (heart-rate) and motion (movement) sensors. That raises the possibility of more frequent, passive detection of concerning readings without new hardware , though Google notes the tool is not a substitute for clinical evaluation.

## The details

- Built by Google Research, the model uses only pulse and motion data from a standard smartwatch , no cuff or additional devices.  
- Tested in a study of 196 people.  
- Reported detection rate in that study: 65.8%.  
- Google reported that this detection rate outperformed traditional in‑office blood pressure measurement in the study.  
- The capability is already integrated into the Google Health app.  
- Google states the tool does not replace a formal medical diagnosis.

What the source does not specify: the summary does not include the study’s population details (age, health status, diversity), the exact smartwatch models or sensors used, other performance metrics such as false positives or negatives, how the AI’s predictions were calibrated against cuff measurements, peer review status, or any regulatory approvals.

## What to watch

Look for external validation and more complete performance reporting , such as sensitivity, specificity, and how the model performs across different demographic groups — before clinical use expands. Also watch for details about which devices and operating systems are supported, and for any regulatory review or guidance about consumer-facing blood pressure screening tools.
